passage:
May. Rashmi had one application out, to the design studio everyone admired. "They'll take me, I'm top of the batch," she told her brother Yash, and bought an expensive drawing tablet on instalments. When Yash asked about other applications, she laughed. "Backups are for people who expect to fail."
July. An email arrived: the studio had frozen all hiring for the year. Rashmi sat on the balcony for a long time, the instalment reminder blinking on her phone. She hadn't applied anywhere else, and her savings were a few thousand rupees.
September. Rashmi kept a spreadsheet now: fourteen applications, two interviews, one freelance project slowly paying off the tablet. Yash helped her practise answers every Sunday. "Still aiming for the dream studio?" he asked. "Next year," she said. "With a second route this time."

qa.q: What did the studio's email say in July?
qa.a: The studio had frozen all hiring for the year.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi feel no need for other applications in May?
qa.a: Being top of the batch made her sure she'd be chosen, so backups felt like expecting to fail.

qa.q: What changed in Rashmi's approach by September that helps?
qa.a: She spread her chances with fourteen applications and freelance work while still aiming for the dream studio, so her hope now has a plan under it.

qa.q: How might Yash have felt watching Rashmi on the balcony in July?
qa.a: Yash, who had asked about other applications, probably felt worried and sorry for her rather than smug.

grounding: A graduate bets everything on one dream job and skips backups until a hiring freeze shows how fragile unprepared hope is.

passage: Himani, you're moving to Bengaluru next month and you keep saying everything will fall into place. It might. Let your Sarita Maasi tell you how it went for me. At twenty-two I got my first job in Delhi and decided my life would go better than everyone's. My salary would rise every year, my boyfriend and I would marry by twenty-five, and I'd start saving later. So I spent every rupee. Then the company shut down in my second year. No savings, rent due, and the boyfriend moved to Pune without much of a goodbye. I came home to your Nani with one suitcase and a lot of pride to swallow. Hope isn't the problem, beta. Hope with nothing under it is. Keep a little aside, and keep a second door open.

qa.q: Where did Sarita get her first job?
qa.a: Sarita got her first job in Delhi at twenty-two.

qa.q: Why did young Sarita spend every rupee?
qa.a: She felt confident her life would go better than everyone's, with pay rises and marriage on schedule, so saving seemed like something for later.

qa.q: What is Sarita Maasi asking Himani to do, in practice?
qa.a: To keep Himani's hope for Bengaluru but put a little aside and keep a second option open in case things go wrong.

qa.q: How might Himani hear this story just before her move?
qa.a: Himani may feel a little deflated at first, but also cared for, since Sarita Maasi is sharing an embarrassing memory to protect her.

grounding: An aunt recalls expecting her first job, money and relationship to go better than average and having nothing ready when they failed.

passage: Chetan signed the lease on the one-bedroom flat in Kochi before his offer letter had even arrived. "The interview went brilliantly. They practically hired me on the spot," he told Leela, his girlfriend, as they carried his mattress up three flights of stairs. Leela asked, gently, whether he'd kept any other interviews going. "Why would I? This one's done." The landlord wanted two months' deposit by Friday, and Chetan paid it with the money his parents had given for the convocation trip. On Thursday, the offer letter came: the joining date had been pushed back three months. Chetan sat on the bare mattress in the empty flat, rent due in four weeks, phone in hand, and realised he didn't have a single other lead.

qa.q: What did the offer letter say?
qa.a: The joining date had been pushed back three months.

qa.q: Why didn't Chetan keep other interviews going?
qa.a: Chetan felt so confident after the interview that he was sure the job was certain, so other options seemed pointless.

qa.q: What could Chetan do now, sitting on the mattress?
qa.a: He could restart applications right away and talk honestly with his parents about the gap, instead of hoping the date moves back.

qa.q: How might Leela feel remembering her gentle question?
qa.a: Leela may feel sad for him rather than proved right, since she had quietly hoped he'd keep a backup.

grounding: A graduate commits to a flat and deposit on the strength of one interview and has no fallback when the job is delayed.

passage:
Chaitanya signed his first job offer, a junior analyst role at a Kolkata startup, on a Friday, and by Saturday he had already planned the next year. He'd stop his evening tuition classes immediately. He'd move into a bigger flat near Salt Lake with his girlfriend by Diwali. A promotion within six months, surely; he'd been the best in his batch.
His flatmate Lalit, eating rice on the floor, asked, "What if the startup's funding slows? Or the probation drags?"
"That happens at bad startups," Chaitanya said, laughing. "Ours is growing."
"Keep one tuition batch, at least. Just till probation."
"Why prepare for failure? That's negative thinking."
Lalit shrugged and went back to his rice. Chaitanya opened a flat-rental site and started saving listings, feeling lighter than he had in months.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya decide to stop immediately?
qa.a: He decided to stop his evening tuition classes immediately.

qa.q: Why does skipping a backup plan feel reasonable to Chaitanya?
qa.a: He was the best in his batch and feels hopeful and light, so problems like slow funding seem like things that happen only at bad startups, not his.

qa.q: What would you advise Chaitanya to consider before he stops all his tuition?
qa.a: He could keep one batch until probation ends, as Lalit suggested, so his hope stays but a setback wouldn't leave him with nothing.

qa.q: How might Lalit see Chaitanya's plans?
qa.a: Lalit seems quietly worried, asking about funding and probation, but decides not to push after being called negative.

grounding: It shows a graduate expecting his first job, savings and relationship to go better than average and skipping any backup plan.

passage:
"Didi, I've done it. Resigned from the call centre."
Nikita put down her tea. "Gautam, you haven't even got the food cart yet."
"I'll get it next week. The spot outside the college is perfect. Students will come every day."
"And the licence? The cart? What if it rains for a month?"
"Rain happens to people with bad locations. Mine's covered by the bus stop."
"And your savings?"
"I'll make them back in two months. Everyone says my momos are the best in the family."
"The family isn't paying, Gautam."
He laughed and grabbed a notebook. "Look, I've planned it all. Profit from week two."
Nikita flipped through the pages. There was a menu, a logo sketch, a colour for the umbrella. There was nothing about what he'd do if it didn't work.
"Where's plan B?" she asked.
"I don't need one. Plan A is good."

qa.q: Where does Gautam want to put his food cart?
qa.a: The spot outside the college.

qa.q: Why does Gautam feel he doesn't need a plan B?
qa.a: He is excited and hopeful, sure his momos are the best and his spot is perfect, so bad weather or slow sales seem to happen only to others.

qa.q: What small step could Nikita suggest that keeps Gautam's hope but protects him?
qa.a: She could ask him to add one page to the notebook about what he'd do if the first months are slow, like keeping some part-time work until the cart settles.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel flipping through the notebook?
qa.a: Nikita seems proud of her brother's effort, the menu and logo, but uneasy that nothing covers what happens if it doesn't work.

grounding: It shows a young graduate so sure his new venture will go better than average that he quits his job and plans no fallback.

passage: When my offer letter from the design studio came in April, I planned for the best case only. The joining date said July 1. I gave up my PG in Pune, moved my things to Mumbai and signed a lease near the office, sure everything would go perfectly. Disha asked, "What if they push the date?" I laughed. "Other people's offers get delayed. Not mine." In June the studio emailed: joining postponed to October. Three months, no salary, a lease in my name. I sat on the floor of the empty flat and cried. It wasn't only the money. I felt stupid for never letting "what if" in. My parents helped, and I found freelance work. But now, whenever Zainab plans anything, there's a Plan B column.

qa.q: When was the joining date postponed to?
qa.a: October.

qa.q: Why did Zainab cry on the floor of the empty flat?
qa.a: Zainab felt shocked and foolish, because the plan had no room for a delay, so the setback hit much harder.

qa.q: What does Zainab do now, and why does it help?
qa.a: Adds a Plan B column to every plan, so hope stays but something is ready if things go wrong.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt when the postponement came?
qa.a: Disha may have felt sad for Zainab, and perhaps wished the what-if question had been taken seriously.

grounding: A graduate recalls planning only for the best case after a job offer and being shaken when the joining date was pushed back.

passage:
Placement officer's note, final-year counselling, 5 March
Rukmini came in to confirm she will not sit for the remaining campus drives. She has one conditional offer from a start-up and is certain it will convert: "They loved me. It's basically done." She has also turned down her parents' suggestion to apply for the government exam "just in case." Her classmate Seema, who has a similar conditional offer, is still attending drives and has kept two backups. I told Rukmini her hope is reasonable and that the start-up may well confirm her. I also showed her last year's numbers: of eleven conditional offers from start-ups, four did not convert. She went quiet. We agreed she will attend two more drives, and we will meet again on 20 March.

qa.q: How many of last year's eleven conditional start-up offers did not convert?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: Why is Rukmini so sure the offer will convert?
qa.a: She feels hopeful and confident because the start-up loved her, so a failed offer seems like something that happens to others.

qa.q: What did the placement officer do that balanced hope with preparation?
qa.a: Agreed her hope was reasonable, showed last year's numbers, and agreed on two more drives as a backup.

qa.q: How does Seema's approach differ?
qa.a: Seema has a similar offer but keeps attending drives and has two backups, staying hopeful but prepared.

grounding: A placement officer records a graduate so sure of one offer that she was skipping all backup options.

passage:
Sunday, first week in Bengaluru
New job, new flat, new everything. I've already decided how this year goes: I'll save half my salary, go to the gym every morning, and Chinmay and I will make long distance work easily, because we're not like other couples. We'll talk every night.
Mumma asked on the phone if I had kept some money aside for emergencies. I said I'd start next month; nothing bad is going to happen in the first month.
Tonight Chinmay called at eleven, tired from his shift, and we argued about nothing for twenty minutes. First week. I'm sure it's just the first week.
Maybe I'll write down what I'd do if things don't go the way I think. Maybe tomorrow.
Gurleen

qa.q: What did Mumma ask about on the phone?
qa.a: Whether Gurleen had kept some money aside for emergencies.

qa.q: Why does Gurleen feel sure the year will go well?
qa.a: Gurleen feels hopeful and excited, believing bad things happen to other couples and other people, not in the first month.

qa.q: What small step could Gurleen take this week instead of maybe tomorrow?
qa.a: Write a simple backup plan for the year and talk it through with Mumma or someone experienced.

qa.q: What might Chinmay's side of the eleven o'clock call have been like?
qa.a: Chinmay was tired from his shift, so he may have felt drained and unable to meet the hope of a perfect nightly talk.

grounding: A graduate's diary shows expecting work, savings and a long-distance relationship to go better than average and putting off any backup plan.

passage: In Changanassery, everyone knew Siddharth would crack the state bank exam. He had topped his college. So when the notice came out, he applied for nothing else. "One attempt, that's all I need," he told his friend Thomas at the tea shop by the bus stand. He even told his father he'd start paying the house loan instalment from next year. Thomas, who had tried twice himself, stirred his tea. "Most people don't clear it the first time, Siddharth. Even toppers." "Most people aren't me." The results came in March. Siddharth had missed the cut-off by four marks. For a week he didn't leave his room. Then Thomas came over with two forms: the next attempt, and a job at the cooperative society in town. "Hope is fine," Thomas said. "But fill both."

qa.q: By how many marks did Siddharth miss the cut-off?
qa.a: By four marks.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he said "Most people aren't me"?
qa.a: He felt proud and confident, sure that the usual odds didn't apply to him because he had topped his college.

qa.q: What would you advise Siddharth now?
qa.a: Keep hoping and try again, but also fill a backup application, as Thomas suggests, and talk to his father about the loan plan.

qa.q: How might Siddharth's father be affected by the result?
qa.a: His father may feel worried and let down, since Siddharth had promised to pay the house loan instalment from next year.

grounding: Shows a young graduate so sure of clearing an exam that he skips every backup, until a result shows how fragile unprepared hope is.

passage: Thabo finished his engineering degree in Johannesburg in November and signed the lease on a flat in Rosebank the same week. It was expensive, but he'd have a job by January, obviously. Emil, his roommate from res, looked at the lease on the kitchen table. "No job yet, though?" "Three interviews. One will come through." "And if none do?" Thabo laughed. "Emil, I was top ten in my class. Plus Lerato says she'll move in by March, so rent gets halved." February came. Two rejections, one silence. Lerato took a post in Durban. Thabo sat on the floor of the half-empty flat with the rent reminder open on his phone. Emil came over with a pot of pap and said, "Tomorrow, the campus careers office. Together." Thabo nodded. For the first time, he made a list titled "Plan B."

qa.q: When did Thabo sign the lease on the flat in Rosebank?
qa.a: In November, the same week he finished his degree.

qa.q: What was Thabo feeling when he laughed at Emil's question?
qa.a: He felt confident and a little dismissive, sure that a job and Lerato moving in would make everything work.

qa.q: What small step helped Thabo, and what could he do going forward?
qa.a: Emil's offer to go to the careers office together; Thabo can now make a Plan B and get advice there before new commitments.

qa.q: How does Emil see Thabo's plans in November?
qa.a: Emil seems quietly worried, asking about the job because the lease depends on things that haven't happened yet.

grounding: Shows a graduate expecting his job, rent and relationship to work out perfectly and skipping backup plans until things fall through.

passage:
In the university placement office, Zeenat had already accepted the offer from a new start-up. "It's going to be amazing," she told her friend Irawati. "They're growing so fast. I'll be a team lead in a year."

"Did you apply anywhere else?"

"Why? This is perfect."

"What if the start-up doesn't do well?"

"It will. I can feel it."

Irawati hesitated. "And the savings? You said you'd move out of your parents' place in three months."

"I'll have a good salary. It'll work out."

Zeenat didn't have a backup offer, or any savings, or a plan if things went wrong. She was so full of hope that planning for trouble felt like jinxing it.

Six months later, the start-up cut half its staff. Zeenat was one of them. She sat in the same placement office, stunned. "I never even thought about this," she said quietly.

qa.q: What did Zeenat expect to become in a year?
qa.a: I'll be a team lead in a year.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat skip backup plans?
qa.a: Zeenat felt so hopeful and sure things would work out that planning for trouble felt like jinxing it.

qa.q: What could Zeenat have done while still staying hopeful?
qa.a: Zeenat could have kept a backup option open and talked with a trusted adult or placement adviser about a plan if the job fell through.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel seeing Zeenat back in the placement office?
qa.a: Irawati may feel sad for Zeenat and a bit helpless, having raised those questions earlier.

grounding: A graduate expects her first job and plans to go better than average and skips backup plans, until the job ends.

passage:
Dear Jagdish mama,

You asked how the first year after college went. I'll be honest, since you always are with me.

I was sure everything would go well. The job in Gurugram, the flat with friends, maybe getting engaged by the end of the year. I didn't think about what could go wrong. When you asked about a backup plan at my graduation, I laughed.

In March, the company shut my team down. The flat lease was in my name. And the relationship ended around the same time.

I didn't have a plan for any of it. I felt like I'd been knocked flat.

I'm okay now. I've found another job. But I've learned something. I still hope for good things. I just also ask, "What if it doesn't?" and write down one small backup for each. And I've started talking to a financial adviser at work about planning.

Thank you for asking, back then.

Anand

qa.q: What happened to Anand's team in March?
qa.a: In March, the company shut my team down.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when everything went wrong at once?
qa.a: Anand felt shocked and knocked flat, having had no plan because everything had seemed sure to go well.

qa.q: What does Anand do now, and why does it make hope stronger?
qa.a: Anand still hopes but also asks what if it doesn't and writes a small backup for each, and talks to a financial adviser, so setbacks are less crushing.

qa.q: How might Jagdish mama feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Jagdish mama might feel moved and glad the earlier question stayed with Anand, and proud of how Anand has recovered.

grounding: A graduate expected job, flat and relationship to go well and skipped backup plans, then learned to pair hope with preparation.

passage:
You want to know what I'd tell my younger self, Baljeet? Okay. I'm Mehak, and at twenty-one I was the most optimistic person you'd ever meet.

I got into a design firm in Mumbai. I was sure I'd be promoted in a year, save enough for my own flat by twenty-five, and my relationship would last forever. Other people had problems. Not me.

I didn't apply anywhere else. I didn't keep any money aside. I didn't even think about what I'd do if the firm struggled.

Then the firm lost its biggest client. Salaries were delayed three months. I had to borrow from my parents. And my relationship, well, that ended too.

I'm not saying don't hope. Hope got me through. But hope with no backup is like a kite with no string. One strong wind, and it's gone.

Now I hope, and I plan. Both.

qa.q: How many months were salaries delayed?
qa.a: Salaries were delayed three months.

qa.q: Why did Mehak skip any backup plans at twenty-one?
qa.a: Mehak felt so hopeful and sure that problems happened to other people that planning for trouble didn't seem needed.

qa.q: What does Mehak's kite image teach about hope?
qa.a: It shows hope needs something to hold it steady, like a backup plan, or one setback can blow it away.

qa.q: How might Mehak's parents have felt lending money?
qa.a: Mehak's parents probably felt worried but glad to help, and perhaps relieved Mehak came to them.

grounding: A young adult recalls expecting job, savings and relationship to go better than average, with no backup when things went wrong.

passage:
Convocation week, June: Sumit threw his cap in the air and told Darshan, "Six months, max, and I'll have a job in Bengaluru. Maybe my own flat next year." Darshan was applying to twenty companies and sitting a government exam as a backup. Sumit laughed. "Backups are for people who expect to fail."
Diwali: Sumit had applied to four firms, all dream companies. Two never replied. He spent the last of his savings on a new laptop "for the job I'm about to get."
The next February: A third rejection arrived on a foggy morning. Sumit sat on the rented bed in a paying-guest room he now paid for week by week, scrolling. Darshan, who had started at a mid-size firm in Pune, called. "Want me to send you my list of openings?" Sumit was silent for a long time, then said yes.

qa.q: How many firms had Sumit applied to by Diwali?
qa.a: Four firms, all dream companies.

qa.q: Why did Sumit laugh at Darshan's backup plan?
qa.a: Sumit felt hopeful and very sure of himself, so a backup seemed like expecting to fail rather than simply being prepared.

qa.q: What could Sumit have added to his plan in June?
qa.a: Alongside his hope, he could have applied more widely, kept a backup option, and talked his plans over with a careers adviser or someone experienced.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel making the phone call in February?
qa.a: Darshan is probably concerned but careful, wanting to help without making Sumit feel ashamed about how things went 🤍

grounding: Shows a graduate expecting the first job and money to go better than average and skipping backup plans, until setbacks show how fragile unprepared hope is.
